# How the Course Works

This class is a workshop. Each week has the same rhythm:

1. **Quiz.** Class starts with a short, handwritten quiz on the previous week.
2. **Concept.** We learn one new idea (how LLMs work, what an agent is, how to
   inject data into a document, etc.).
3. **Build together.** We use that idea in class to make something, hands-on.
4. **Build at home.** You take the idea further on your own in that week's
   [build](#builds), due the following week.

Each week pairs a **concept** (the idea we learn) with a **building** (the kind of
thing we make). Some buildings span several weeks. For example, we work on
websites in Weeks 3 through 5, and each week adds a new idea on top of the last.
The [schedule](schedule.qmd) lists both for every week.

The semester moves in three stages:

- **Weeks 1-2: Foundations, no agents.** We use chat-based AI tools, learn how
  LLMs work, and learn Git and GitHub by hand.
- **Weeks 3-5: Agents and websites.** We bring in AI coding agents and build and
  deploy websites. In Week 5 we switch to the workflow we use for the rest of the
  semester.
- **Weeks 6-15: New things to build.** Each week adds a new skill and a new kind
  of artifact: writing, images, animation, sound, data-driven documents, PDFs,
  data visualizations, and slides. You'll also work on your
  [final project](#final-project) in the second half of the semester.

## Agent → code → artifact

From Week 5 on, we build everything the same way. **The agent writes the code, you
run the code, and the code builds the artifact.** We don't ask the AI to hand us
the finished website, image, or PDF directly. Building through code gives you
something you can reproduce, it uses far fewer tokens, and it gives you control:
if you want to change one thing, you change one line of code instead of
re-rolling the whole thing and hoping.

## You control Git

Git is how you know what an agent changed. In this class **you always control Git
yourself, through [GitHub Desktop](https://desktop.github.com/download/). Never
let the agent make commits for you.** Review what the agent changed (the diff in
GitHub Desktop), check that it works, and then commit it yourself with a message
that says what changed.

# Assignments

## Participation & Attendance

**Attendance will be taken** and will be part of your participation grade.

In-person attendance is critical as we will spend most of class building things
together. You should plan to attend class in person each week.

**There will be no option for remote attendance (e.g. zoom)**, and class sessions
will not be recorded. If you have any questions or need special accommodations,
send me a message on slack and we can discuss. If you must miss class for an
excused absence (e.g. medical issue), please message Professor Helveston and get
notes from your fellow classmates.

Multiple absences, inappropriate or unprofessional behavior during class (such as
monopolizing discussions or being rude or disruptive), not participating in
classroom exercises, and not being prepared for class will result in a poor score
for attendance and participation.

## Quizzes

There will be **13 short quizzes**, one at the start of every class from Week 2
on (check the [schedule](schedule.qmd)). Quizzes are **handwritten** on paper,
with no devices or notes. They are **conceptual**: they test whether you
understand the ideas from the previous week (what a token is, what a commit
records, why an agent shouldn't retype your data), not whether you can write code
from memory.

Quizzes are **short** (10 minutes) and are designed to test for fluency and to
demonstrate where additional study is needed. Your **lowest two are dropped**. If
you do poorly on one or two, use that as feedback on where you need additional
improvement.

**The best way to ensure you do well on quizzes is to be active in class and
complete your builds on time.**

**Make up quizzes are not available**. If you arrive late, you can take the quiz
in the remaining time left, but you will not be given additional time. Make ups
will only be allowed for excused absences that are discussed and agreed upon with
the professor _prior_ to class. If you contact the professor after class for a
make up, it will not be granted unless a true emergency prevented you from
attending class that could not have been communicated earlier.

> **Why quiz at all?** Research shows that giving small quizzes throughout a class
> can dramatically help with *retention*. It's a phenomenon known as the
> "retrieval effect" - basically, you have to _practice_ remembering things,
> otherwise your brain won't remember them. The phenomenon and research on it is
> explained in detail in the book
> ["Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning,"](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780674729018)
> by Brown, Roediger, and McDaniel.

## Builds

Each week from Week 1 through Week 13 there is a take-home **build**: you use that
week's concept to make something on your own. There are 13 builds in total, and
your **lowest build score is dropped**.

Every build is submitted as a GitHub repository that includes:

- the build itself (from Week 5 on, the code that renders your artifact, not
  just the artifact);
- the **transcript** of your work with the AI (your prompts, its responses, and
  your iterations);
- from Build 5 on, a short **token usage report** (we'll learn how to measure this
  in Week 5).

Builds are graded on a 0 / 0.5 / 1 scale using the [build rubric](#build-rubric).
You may discuss approaches with your classmates, but every build is your own work.

## Final Project

The final project is **individual**: everyone builds their own project of their
own design, using the workflow and the kinds of things we've built during the
semester. We introduce the project in Week 8 so you have time to think about it.
There are two deliverables:

- **Proposal** (due Oct 27). A short, high-level description of what you want to
  build. It's graded for completion (1 if you submit it, 0 if you don't). Its
  purpose is to get you feedback early on whether your idea is a good one and
  whether it's well scoped.
- **Final submission** (due Dec 8). A link to a GitHub repository with your
  project and all of its source files, your transcripts, a token usage report,
  and a **5-minute video** about your project posted to YouTube. In Week 15 we'll
  learn to build slide decks, which you can use in your video. Graded 0 / 0.5 / 1
  using the [final project rubric](#final-project-rubric).

I'll grade the projects before the final exam, and we'll start the exam period by
showcasing a few of them. View the [final project overview](project/0-overview.qmd)
page for more details.

## Final Exam

There will be a **handwritten final exam** during the final exam period (date set
by the registrar). Like the quizzes, it is conceptual and done on paper with no
devices or notes, and it covers material from the entire semester. We'll start
the exam period with the final project showcase, then take the exam.

## Category Breakdown

Final grades will be calculated as follows:

<div style="width:650px">

Item                        | Weight | Notes
----------------------------|--------|-------------------------------------
Participation / Attendance  | 5%     | (Yes, I take attendance)
Builds (13)                 | 25%    | 0 / 0.5 / 1 each, lowest dropped
Quizzes (13)                | 25%    | Handwritten, lowest two dropped
Final Project: Proposal     | 2%     | Graded for completion (1 / 0)

## How Builds Are Graded

I want to be upfront about this: **most of the build grading is done by Claude.**
For each build, Claude reads your repository, your transcript, and your token
report, checks your work against the rubric below, and drafts a score and
feedback. I review those drafts and make the final call. If you think a grade is
wrong, ask for a [re-grade](#re-grades) and I'll look at it myself.

This is also why your transcript matters so much. It's the record of how you
worked: what you asked for, what you checked, and what you changed.

## Build Rubric {#build-rubric}

<div style="width:750px">

Score | Meaning | What it looks like
------|---------|--------------------------------------------------------------
**1** | Complete | Every required part of the build is there and works. From Build 5 on, the artifact is built by code in your repo, and anyone could re-run that code to get it back. Your transcript is included and shows you directing the agent, reviewing its work, and iterating. You made the commits yourself, in reasonable steps, with messages that say what changed. From Build 5 on, your token usage report is included.
**0.5** | Partial | A real attempt, but something important is missing or broken. For example: a required part is missing, the artifact doesn't run or render, the transcript or token report is missing, the agent made the commits, or all the work is in one giant commit.
**0** | Missing | Nothing submitted, or no real attempt (e.g., the submission has nothing to do with the assignment).

</div>

## Final Project Rubric {#final-project-rubric}

The final project is graded on **effort**: did you take on a real project and see
it through?

<div style="width:750px">

Score | Meaning | What it looks like
------|---------|--------------------------------------------------------------
**1** | Strong effort | The project is ambitious for its scope (including any changes we agreed on from your proposal feedback) and it's finished. The artifacts are built from source files in your repo using the agent → code → artifact workflow. The 5-minute video clearly shows what you made, how you made it, and what you learned. Transcripts and a token usage report are included.
**0.5** | Some effort | The project is submitted but is small for its scope, mostly unfinished, or doesn't build from the repo, **or** one of the deliverables (repo, video, transcripts, token report) is missing.
**0** | Missing | Nothing submitted, or minimal effort.

</div>

## Grading Scale

<div style="width:400px">
Grade  | Range       | Grade | Range
-------|-------------|-------|------------
A      | 94 - 100%   | C     | 74 - 76.99%
A-     | 90 - 93.99% | C-    | 70 - 73.99%
B+     | 87 - 89.99% | D+    | 67 - 69.99%
B      | 84 - 86.99% | D     | 64 - 66.99%
B-     | 80 - 83.99% | D-    | 60 - 63.99%
C+     | 77 - 79.99% | F     | < 60%
</div>

The course instructors may choose to change the scales at their discretion. You
are guaranteed that your letter grade will never become worse as a result of
changing scales.

## Rounding

**I do not round final grades**. Here's why. Wherever the line is drawn, there
will always be students just below or just above, and rounding will only move that
bar and create another group of students who are just below and just above.
Rounding does not eliminate the issue but rather just shifts it to another group
of students. This is why I draw the lines before the course starts - to ensure a
fair and transparent system for everyone, that way you don't have to shoot for a
moving bar. To be clear, this means I will not modify or round your final score,
even if you're _very close_ to a different letter grade (e.g., a 93.98 is an "A-"
and will not be rounded up to an "A").

Rather than round, I grade generously throughout the semester. For example, if you
give a quiz your best shot and completely fail it, you will likely get a 50%
instead of a 0%. The 50% is for trying as learning still happens when you try
regardless if you get the question correct (0s are reserved for those who simply
don't attempt it).

# AI Tools and Cost

You'll need two things that aren't free: an AI coding agent and, starting in
Week 7, an API key for generating images. **Check Slack before you pay for
anything.** We are pursuing institutional access, and I'll post there if we get
it. If the cost is a barrier for you, let me know.

## An AI coding agent (about $20/month)

I will use and teach [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/quickstart) in
class, which requires at least a [Claude Pro](https://claude.ai/login?plan=pro)
subscription (about $20/month). You're welcome to use an alternative, such as
[Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) (free with a Google
account) or [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) (needs a paid ChatGPT plan).
The underlying skills transfer, but in-class instruction and course materials
assume Claude Code, so you're on your own for translating anything tool-specific.

**Why a subscription and not the API?** Agents burn through a lot of tokens.
Paying per token through an API would cost far more than a flat monthly
subscription.

## An image-generation API key (Week 7 on)

We don't use Claude to make images. Starting in Week 7, your agent will call
Google's image model (Nano Banana) through the
[Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/image-generation). This is paid
per image, but if you're careful it should only add up to a few dollars over the
semester. We'll set up API keys in class, including how to keep them secret
(never in your code, never in a commit).

# Course Policies

## tl;dr

- BE NICE
- BE ON TIME
- BE HONEST
- DON'T CHEAT
- SERIOUSLY: DON'T CHEAT

## Late Policy

Each student is allowed **3** late build submissions - use them however you want,
no questions asked.
These are meant to cover illness, family emergencies, and religious holidays.

Beyond those, all other assignments are due by 11:59pm on the assigned due date
unless specified otherwise. Assignments submitted up to 24 hours past this
deadline will be graded to a max of half credit (0.5 on the 0 / 0.5 / 1 scale).
Assignments submitted beyond 24 hours past the deadline will not be graded and
will be assigned a 0. The final project cannot use a late submission, since I need
time to grade the projects before the final exam.

If you need a special accommodation such as due to an illness, family emergency,
or religious holidays, contact the instructor ahead of time.

## Re-grades

You may request a re-grade within 7 days of receiving a grade, including any grade
that Claude drafted. Send me a message on Slack with the assignment name and what
you think was graded incorrectly and why. I'll review your submission against the
rubric myself. If I find an error, I'll fix the grade. If not, the original grade
stands.

## Use of AI

Using AI in this course is **required**. It's the core skill being taught. Every build and the final project must be made with AI, and
you must submit your transcripts.

Now, LLMs are pretty good, but sometimes they suck. **Don't blindly trust them** -
they will betray you. You are fully responsible for everything you submit, so
read what the agent produces, run it, look at the result, and fix it when it's
wrong. That's what the verification loops we learn in Week 8 are for.

There are three places where AI is **not** allowed, each for a reason:

- **Week 1 and Build 1 (Git by hand).** You can't supervise an agent that changes
  your files until you understand version control yourself.
- **Git, all semester.** The agent never makes commits for you (see
  [You control Git](#you-control-git)). Your commits are how you show that you
  reviewed what the agent did.
- **Quizzes and the final exam.** These are handwritten, with no devices, because
  they test what *you* understand.

Your transcripts are read by Claude (for grading) and by me, and are used only
for grading this course. Before you submit, remove API keys, passwords, and any
personal information from them.

I don't use AI-detection software (it's unreliable). The record of your work is
your transcript and your Git history. I also use AI myself, to help prepare course
materials and to draft build grades and feedback, and I review everything before
you see it.

Throughout the course we'll talk about where AI fails, what it costs (in money and
energy), copyright and authorship, and when *not* to use it.

> Curious how LLMs actually work? That's Week 2. If you want a head start, check
> out [this article](https://www.understandingai.org/p/large-language-models-explained-with),
> which provides a simplified description of how they work (which itself is still
> quite complicated).

## Cheating

Cheating results in a penalty on the first offense, and failing the course on the
second offense. Cheating on builds and the final project can include:

- Submitting someone else's work or transcript as your own, in any amount.
- Editing a transcript to hide or fake what happened. (Removing secrets and
  personal information is fine and expected.)
- Providing your builds or transcripts to anyone else in the class.
- Putting solutions to course assignments online.
- Getting someone else to do the assignment for you.

Cheating on quizzes or the final exam can include:

- Referring to any external resources while completing it (phones, notes, AI
  tools, etc.).
- Copying part of an answer off of another student's paper, even if it is very
  small.
- Using solutions provided by students who previously took the course.

### Penalties

Violations will be reported to the
[Office of Student Rights & Responsibilities](https://studentconduct.gwu.edu/charging-academic-integrity-violations).
Penalties are decided by the course instructors, and can vary based on the
severity of the offense. Possible penalties include:

- Receiving a 0 on the assignment/quiz in question.
- Receiving a full letter grade deduction in the course.
- Automatically failing the course.

Depending on the student's prior academic history, violations may also be
accompanied by a letter to the Dean of Student Affairs, again at the instructors'
discretion. This can lead to university-level penalties, such as being suspended
or expelled.

### Grace Period

College is a time when you do a lot of learning. Sometimes, you might make bad
decisions or mistakes. The most important thing for you to do is to learn from
your mistakes, to constantly grow, and become a better person.

Sometimes, students panic and copy someone else's work right before the deadline,
then regret what they did afterwards. Therefore, you may rescind any build
submission for up to 24 hours after the deadline with no questions asked. Simply
message the course instructors asking to delete the submission in question, and we
will do so. Deleted submissions will not be graded. However, it will always be
better to get a 0 (or partial credit) on an assignment than to get a cheating
violation!
